messages.body_plain:
Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> writes:

> I think just talking about diff-eqs is going to scare
> most people off.

That's a big reason why SD modelers almost always write integral
equations; they somehow seem more intuitive, and they seem more directly
related to what's going on in the world (I'm adding something here to
this stock [state variable], and I'm taking something away over there.).

Bill
--
Bill Harris
Facilitated Systems
http://makingsense.facilitatedsystems.com/

messages.subject: tests need to be more robust
messages.subject_clean: tests need to be more robust
messages.body_plain:
Is there any way to try to fix the tests so that they don't fail
for reasons unrelated to the pull requests?  It's very frustrating
from a developer perspective and is one of the main reasons we can't
quickly merge pull requests.

Maybe we can push the model tests back to something more like a continuous
integration and something not related to each pull request?

The real danger, though, is that I just pretty much ignore failures
because of the overwhelming numbers of false positives.  I only
start getting worried about them when there's a release imminent, like
now.

- Bob

this one.

- Bob

messages.subject: Fwd: python/pandas quickstart
messages.body_plain:
Forwarded from Ido.  I barely have time to get through
my e-mail each day, much less start playing with new
interfaces.  But it does seem an ipython notebook would
be a nice interface for an online Stan manual.

- Bob

 From Ido:

Please feel free to pass this around, I don't have everyone else's emails:

Install Python 2.x, then:

$ virtualenv venv
$ source venv/bin/activate
(virtualenv)$ pip install ipython numpy scipy pandas statsmodels
(virtualenv)$ pip install Theano pymcmc pystan #...
(virtualenv)$ ipython notebook
...it'll load a browser.  Create a notebook and start playing.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as smf
#...do stuff

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Informational Messages
messages.body_plain:
I've been thinking that one solution would be to monitor the # of Metropolis rejections per iteration and if it exceeds a threshold (something like more often than 1 reject in 2-5 iterations), then and only then do we start printing them out.  It's not perfect but at least it should silence things completely for most users but make sure that if it's a serious problem it shows up.

Or, for a third solution, we implement logging and turn off printing these messages by default but we (as above) count the number of rejections per iteration and print it out with the running iteration count.  We can print warnings if it's above threshold (maybe) but also document that the % of rejections should be low and if it's not that users should bump up their log level and explore the issue further.

messages.subject_clean: priors based on condition numbers of matrices
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, February 4, 2014 11:07:18 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I'd like to write a section in the manual on how to put
> a prior on a correlation or covariance matrix based on condition
> number (ratio of highest to lowest eigenvalue).  I've heard people
> talking about it before and was reminded of it when I updated the
> eigendecomposition doc in the manual.
>
> Or is this a terrible idea?

That kind of makes sense if the eigenvalues and eigenvectors were primitive. But we don't have a orthonormal data type for the eigenvectors. To calculate the eigendecomposition in order to express a prior on the condition number in order to imply a prior on the matrix seems complicated.

> Am I right in reading the Matrix Cookbook (Nov 15 2012 version) section 2.3 (Derivatives
> of Eigenvalues, page 10) as saying I won't need a Jacobian adjustment?
>
>    For symmetric A with real eigenvalues lambda_i and eigenvectors v_i, they say
>
>      partial lambda_i = v_i' * partial(A) * v_i

That is the right formula for the derivative of the eigenvalue, but there is still a Jacobian adjustment. It is a change-of-variables from covariance matrix space to eigenvector-eigenvalue space, an implicit uniform prior on the eigenvectors, and a prior on the ratio of two (non-independent) eigenvalues that due to the ordering constraint implies some information about the intermediate eigenvalues.

All the priors we have on symmetric positive definite matrices involve a determinant and as long as the exponent on that determinant is positive, then they put zero mass on the singular matrices.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Informational Messages
messages.body_plain:
I agree, some more sophisticated logging/output message control is a good way to go but that only helps if we disable these messages by default and I still stand by that being a dangerous thing to do outright.  For every person that sends worried emails about those messages I'd guess there are quite a few who see them and consequently diagnose some problem in their model.  (I know I've certainly done that more than once!)

My second proposal simply augments the logging solution by adding additional statistics which are less verbose and dire sounding to the output of sampling.  This still gives users a clearly visible statistic which should worry them if it's bad ("why are 90% of my iterations getting Metropolis rejected?  maybe I should turn up by logging level and get more info") but which isn't the HTML equivalent of a BLINK tag.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Tuesday, February 4, 2014 6:57:02 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Ah --- you meant the determinant exponentiated is positive?  Because the
> exponent can definitely be negative if eta in (0,1) --- just like the beta
> distribution as you say.  I had assumed they'd all integrate
> properly to 1, and assumed the singular matrices would get no mass because
> they're a lower-dimensional subspace (and hence measure 0).  Am I still
> missing something here?

That's it pretty much. The singular matrices are an edge case either way but in the absence of data, a chain would run there if 0 < eta < 1. For eta > 1, a chain would stay off the singular subspace, which accomplishes pretty much the same thing as a prior on the condition number.

The condition number is approximately monotonically related to the ratio of the biggest to smallest squared diagonal elements of the Cholesky factor. In the Wishart case, those squared diagonals are chi-squared marginally (with different degrees of freedom) and in the LKJ case, the biggest is 1 and the smallest is an asymmetric beta.

Ben

messages.subject: Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework
messages.body_plain:
We've talked about the need for a statistical testing framework in Stan to ensure that
we're getting reasonable estimates on a variety of test models.  This needs to go
beyond what we currently do in the model tests, which only checks first-order
expectations.

What we really want to do is check the Monte Carlo sampling distribution itself,
in other words that Delta \equiv ( \hat{mu} - mu_{true} ) / MCSE ~ N(0, 1).  This requires that
we have valid estimates of both the Monte Carlo mean, \hat{mu}, and the
Monte Carlo variance and autocorrelation implicit in the MCSE.

The most obvious way to test this would be a simple two-sided Gaussian hypothesis test
for Delta < n for some n \in Z^{+}.  The problem here is that if n is small then we'll get many
false rejections and if n is large then we won't be as sensitive to the shape of the Delta
distribution.

As a more robust test I propose instead the following procedure.

For each model, build up the test by running multiple chains with random initializations.

(Not immediately related to statistical validity, but we would throw in a convergence
test at this point as well).

For each chain compute Delta_{i}.

For n = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} compute a two-sided Binomial test on | Delta_{i} | < n using
the known two-sided Gaussian probabilities. Tune the test to a p-value of 1e-3
to avoid too many rejections.

The hope is that this approach gives us strong sensitivity to the shape of the distribution
of Monte Carlo estimates (both in the bulk and in the tails) without having two many
false rejections that would make incorporating these into any frequently-runt test
a pain.

Thoughts?  Am I doing anything stupid statistically (i.e. is this actually better than
just doing a two-sided Gaussian test directly)?

-Betancourt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Proposal for Statistical Testing Framework
messages.body_plain:
Let me be more clear here.  As I noted in my reply to Bob, I do not want to test for the consistency of the sampled distribution (a sum of point masses)
to the true distribution.  The difficulty in testing the entire distribution (for example KS, or the quantile test in the Cook et al. paper) is that it is
extremely sensitive to convergence and the independence of the samples.  This makes it hard to determine test coverage and tune the tests so that
they reject only when something is wrong.

The more robust measure here is the Monte Carlo Central Limit Theorem, which states that (mean - true) / MCSE ~ N(0, 1).  This incorporates
autocorrelation and is less sensitive to the fine details of convergence.  We also don't want to limit ourselves to a single test because of the difficulty
with the rejection rate, hence the use of an ensemble of chains and turning the whole shebang into a binomial test at various z-scores.

messages.subject: definition of identifiability?
messages.body_plain:
It doesn't look to me like the usual notion of identifiability is right,
at least not in a Bayesian setting.  Both Greene's book where I just read
this and the Wikipedia define identifiability as

    theta != theta'  if and only if   p(theta) != p(theta')

That is, the probability function is one-to-one.

But that can't be right.  If we have parameters mu and sigma for a normal
model with some data y, then let mu* and sigma* be the MLE.

Then if mu != mu*, there must be some sigma != sigma* such that

   p(mu,sigma*) = p(mu*,sigma)

We know this because of continuity and that p(mu,sigma) is bounded
between 0 and p(mu*,sigma*).

So how do I really define identifiability?

Also, is it kosher to use the term "weakly identifiable" for one
of those normal(0,gazillion) priors?

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] definition of identifiability?
messages.body_plain:
I think you’re misreading the definitions.  Remember, classical identifiably
is in the regime of classical statistics, which means likelihoods!

Identifiability on Wikipedia is defined such that if two likelihood _distributions_
(i.e. we haven’t measured the data yet) are distinct then the parameters
labeling them are distinct.  This means that, provided you measure
enough data, you will be able to discriminate between the two
likelihood distributions (and hence the parameters that label them).

This is not the same as the likelihood _values_ being equal for a given
data set.  Remember, “ensembles of possible data sets” not
“the actual data set that I fricken measured”.

A more intuitive (and I believe equivalent) definition is that in the limit
of infinite data the MLE will converge to a single value equal to the
true parameters.  Multimodality?  Unidentified.  The y ~ N(mu1 + m2, sigma)
example?  Unidentified both with and without a proper prior.

The big difference in Bayesian modeling is that we’re conditioning
on only the measured data so the infinite data limit isn’t as meaningful.
Uncertainty is fine so long as it’s finite.  So I tend to think of a parameter
as being identified if its marginal variance is finite, even if it doesn’t
vanish as the data expands towards infinity.

>From this perspective we can think of identifiability as a spectrum,
from weak (large marginal variance as the data grows) to strong
(small, possibly vanishing marginal variance as as the data grows).

messages.subject: "identifiability" is a tricky concept
messages.body_plain:
Identification is actually a tricky concept and is not so clearly defined.  In the broadest sense, a Bayesian model is identified if the posterior distribution is proper.  Then one can do Bayesian inference and that's that.  No need to require a finite variance or even a finite mean, all that's needed is a finite integral of the probability distribution.

That said, there are some reasons why a stronger definition can be useful:

1.  Weak identification.  Suppose that, with reasonable data, you'd have a posterior with a sd of 1 (or that order of magnitude).  But you have sparse data or collinearity or whatever, and so you have some dimension in your posterior that's really flat, some "ridge" with a sd of 1000.  Then it makes sense to say that this parameter or linear combination of parameters is only weakly identified.  Or one can say that it's identified from the prior but not the likelihood.

So, yes, Bob, as chief rabbi I say it is kosher to refer to weak identifiability.  If we wanted to make the concept more formal, we'd stipulate that the model is expressed in terms of some hyperparameter A which is set to a large value, and that weak identifiability corresponds to nonidentifiability when A -> infinity.

Even there, though, some tricky cases arise.  For example, suppose your model includes a parameter p that is defined on [0,1] and is given a flat prior, and suppose the data don't tell us anything about p, so that our posterior is also U(0,1).  That sounds nonidentified to me, but it does have a finite integral.

2.  Aliasing.  Consider an item response model or mixture model where the direction or labeling is unspecified.  Then you can have 2 or 4 or K! different reflections of the posterior.  Even if all priors are proper, so the full posterior is proper, it contains all these copies so this labeling is not identified in any real sense.

Here, and in general, identification depends not just on the model but also on the data.  So, strictly speaking, one should not talk about an "identifiable model" but rather an 'identifiable fitted model" or "identifiable parameters" within a fitted model.

messages.subject: dump reader is slow (maybe)
messages.body_plain:
Ok, so in looking at Stan performance I've done some profiling of optimization with a few large logistic regression datasets that Bob provided me with.  The results are actually incredibly clear: reading large data files is taking a disproportionate amount of time!

For instance, with K=32 predictors and N=1024 data points, the optima was found after 26 iterations and took 0.148 seconds.  Seems pretty fast, but when profiling that it turns out 82% of that time was spent in the constructor for stan::io::dump, parsing the data.  Going bigger, with K=512 and N=16,384, the optima is found after 60 iterations and takes 52.8 seconds.  Of that ~80% is spent reading the data.

What's not clear yet is whether the dump reader can be made significantly faster or if this is just a fundamental issue with parsing a large ASCII file.  I'm also unsure of how much this affects RStan and PyStan.  Regardless, if we want to start trying to win speed competitions with (Cmd)Stan we need to figure something out here.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Hi--

I'd be interested in making the output of  optimizing()  consistent with the output of stan()/sampling().  I left a comment on Bob's feature request with my thinking so far (https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/41), which is that it might make sense for  optimizing()  to output a 'stanfit' object (but with a different attribute value for the sampler).

But I'd really like to hear what others think the right approach would be.

Bob mentioned that you're hoping to do a major refactor on the command parts of Stan, RStan, and PyStan, so people might want to wait on this until after that. So if this is something it makes sense for me to help with but not until later, that's fine too. (It also seems like maybe a small enough thing that if anyone is in that bit of the code while refactoring something, they might naturally get this done as part of something else. That'd be a good outcome too!)

Since this is my first note to stan-dev, I also wanted to say that I appreciate all the work you're doing, and hopefully it'll make sense for me to help out somehow at some point (whether with this or something else).

Thanks!
David

Just my opinion of keeping it simpler.

messages.subject: Re: "identifiability" is a tricky concept
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, February 6, 2014 10:48:48 AM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Identification is actually a tricky concept and is not so clearly defined.

I agree that a lot of people use the word identification without defining what they mean, but there are no shortage of definitions out there. However, I'm not sure that identification is that helpful a concept for the practical problems we are trying to solve here when providing recommendations on how users should write .stan files.

I think many if not most people that think about identification rigorously have in mind a concept that is pre-statistical. So, for them it is going to sound weird to associate "identification" with problems that arise with a particular sample or a particular computational approach. In economics, the idea of identification of a parameter goes back at least to the Cowles Commission guys, such as in the first couple of papers here

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&q=author%3ATC-Koopmans+identification&btnG=&as_sdt=1%2C33

In causal inference, the idea of identification of an average causal effect is a property of a DAG in Pearl's stuff

http://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/jp_home.html

> In the broadest sense, a Bayesian model is identified if the posterior distribution is proper.  Then one can do Bayesian inference and that's that.  No need to require a finite variance or even a finite mean, all that's needed is a finite integral of the probability distribution.

I don't disagree, but what good is the word "identified"? If the posterior distribution is improper, then there is no Bayesian inference.

> That said, there are some reasons why a stronger definition can be useful:
>
> 1.  Weak identification.  Suppose that, with reasonable data, you'd have a posterior with a sd of 1 (or that order of magnitude).  But you have sparse data or collinearity or whatever, and so you have some dimension in your posterior that's really flat, some "ridge" with a sd of 1000.  Then it makes sense to say that this parameter or linear combination of parameters is only weakly identified.  Or one can say that it's identified from the prior but not the likelihood.

Here again we are running into the problem of other people associating the phrase "weak identification" with a different thing (usually instrumental variable models where the instruments are weak predictors of the variable they are instrumenting for). This paper

http://cowles.econ.yale.edu/~dwka/pub/p1370.pdf

basically is interested in situations where some parameter is not identified iff another parameter is zero. And then they drift the population toward that zero.

> So, yes, Bob, as chief rabbi I say it is kosher to refer to weak identifiability.  If we wanted to make the concept more formal, we'd stipulate that the model is expressed in terms of some hyperparameter A which is set to a large value, and that weak identifiability corresponds to nonidentifiability when A -> infinity.

If we were going to go this route, then it is good to be specific with the definitions but I still don't know if you want to call this situation "weak identifiability".

> Even there, though, some tricky cases arise.  For example, suppose your model includes a parameter p that is defined on [0,1] and is given a flat prior, and suppose the data don't tell us anything about p, so that our posterior is also U(0,1).  That sounds nonidentified to me, but it does have a finite integral.

Do you mean that a particular sample doesn't tell us anything about p or that data are incapable of telling us anything about p? In addition, I think it is helpful to distinguish between situations where
There is a unique maximum likelihood estimator (perhaps with probability 1)
There is not a unique maximum likelihood estimator but the likelihood is not flat everywhere with respect to a parameter proposal
The likelihood is flat everywhere with respect to a parameter proposal
What bothers me about some notion of "computational identifiability" is that a Stan user may be in situation 1 but through some combination of weird priors, bad starting values, too few iterations, finite-precision, particular choice of metric, maladaptation, and / or bad luck can't get one or more chains to converge to the stationary distribution of the parameters. That's a practical problem that Stan users face, but I don't think many people would consider it to be an identification problem.

Maybe something that is somewhat unique to Stan is the idea of identified in the constrained parameter space but not identified in the unconstrained parameter space like we have with uniform sampling on the unit sphere.

> 2.  Aliasing.  Consider an item response model or mixture model where the direction or labeling is unspecified.  Then you can have 2 or 4 or K! different reflections of the posterior.  Even if all priors are proper, so the full posterior is proper, it contains all these copies so this labeling is not identified in any real sense.

This one doesn't bother me as much because you can at least conceptually restrict the parameter space to preclude all but one of the reflections, although whether it is easy to do that in Stan is another matter.

> Here, and in general, identification depends not just on the model but also on the data.  So, strictly speaking, one should not talk about an "identifiable model" but rather an 'identifiable fitted model" or "identifiable parameters" within a fitted model.

Certainly, whether you have computational problems depends on the data, among other things. But to say that identification depends on the data goes against the conventional usage where identification is pre-statistical so we need to think about whether it would be more effective to try to redefine identification or to use other phrases to describe the problems we are trying to overcome.

Ben

> On Feb 6, 2014, at 12:46 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> > I think you're misreading the definitions.  Remember, classical identifiably
> > is in the regime of classical statistics, which means likelihoods!
> >
> > Identifiability on Wikipedia is defined such that if two likelihood _distributions_
> > (i.e. we haven't measured the data yet) are distinct then the parameters
> > labeling them are distinct.  This means that, provided you measure
> > enough data, you will be able to discriminate between the two
> > likelihood distributions (and hence the parameters that label them).
> >
> > This is not the same as the likelihood _values_ being equal for a given
> > data set.  Remember, "ensembles of possible data sets" not
> > "the actual data set that I fricken measured".
> >
> > A more intuitive (and I believe equivalent) definition is that in the limit
> > of infinite data the MLE will converge to a single value equal to the
> > true parameters.  Multimodality?  Unidentified.  The y ~ N(mu1 + m2, sigma)
> > example?  Unidentified both with and without a proper prior.
> >
> > The big difference in Bayesian modeling is that we're conditioning
> > on only the measured data so the infinite data limit isn't as meaningful.
> > Uncertainty is fine so long as it's finite.  So I tend to think of a parameter
> > as being identified if its marginal variance is finite, even if it doesn't
> > vanish as the data expands towards infinity.
> >
> >> From this perspective we can think of identifiability as a spectrum,
> > from weak (large marginal variance as the data grows) to strong
> > (small, possibly vanishing marginal variance as as the data grows).
> >
> > On Feb 5, 2014, at 11:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> >> It doesn't look to me like the usual notion of identifiability is right,
> >> at least not in a Bayesian setting.  Both Greene's book where I just read
> >> this and the Wikipedia define identifiability as
> >>
> >>  theta != theta'  if and only if   p(theta) != p(theta')
> >>
> >> That is, the probability function is one-to-one.
> >>
> >> But that can't be right.  If we have parameters mu and sigma for a normal
> >> model with some data y, then let mu* and sigma* be the MLE.
> >>
> >> Then if mu != mu*, there must be some sigma != sigma* such that
> >>
> >> p(mu,sigma*) = p(mu*,sigma)
> >>
> >> We know this because of continuity and that p(mu,sigma) is bounded
> >> between 0 and p(mu*,sigma*).
> >>
> >> So how do I really define identifiability?
> >>
> >> Also, is it kosher to use the term "weakly identifiable" for one
> >> of those normal(0,gazillion) priors?
> >>
> >> - Bob

messages.subject: rstan memory use
messages.body_plain:
A lot of the memory rstan's fit objects use is sneaking in through the
back door.

I have one fit object that is about 488Mb when saved to disk with
save().  The .Misc object (one of the slots), which is an environment,
occupies 435Mb of that.  The environment itself has only one item, which
doesn't look too big.  So I assume what is happening is that the
enclosing environment, and its enclosing environment, and so on are
getting saved as well.

My understanding is that environments are shared objects, so that
multiple objects referencing the same environment see the same thing,
and do not create copies.  Also, at least some environments (maybe the
base and global environments) are not saved to disk.  I'm not sure if
package environments (imports:rstan is toward the top of the enclosing
environment frames for .Misc) are saved, or simply an indication to load
the appropriate library (since I've noticed that load() can trigger
messages that libraries are being loaded).

My typical usage involves saving fit objects to disk and then reading
them into other processes.  I suspect that this breaks the sharing of
environments, that is a I get one new copy with each object read in.

I don't know if there's anything that can be done about this, but if
there's a way to avoid it that would be nice.

I discovered this because I've been running simulations with multiple
fit objects, and my jobs require a lot of memory, like 16GB.  I have
also been sending some objects between processes (with Rmpi).
environments crop up in a lot of unexpected (to me) places: every
formula has one, and so does a model frame.  And so does a stanfit
object.  So, for example, I have one formula that required 3.5G to save
to disk; it was a couple hundred bytes after I replaced the environment
with one of the canonical ones like emptyenv() or baseenv().  I later
discovered empytenv() was a poor choice since it causes operations on
the formula to fail with messages like "can't find list function".

Ross Boylan

>      > from weak (large marginal variance as the data grows) to strong
>      > (small, possibly vanishing marginal variance as as the data grows).

>      >> this and the Wikipedia define identifiability as
>      >>
>      >>  theta != theta'  if and only if   p(theta) != p(theta')
>      >>
>      >> That is, the probability function is one-to-one.
>      >>
>      >> But that can't be right.  If we have parameters mu and sigma for a normal
>      >> model with some data y, then let mu* and sigma* be the MLE.
>      >>
>      >> Then if mu != mu*, there must be some sigma != sigma* such that
>      >>
>      >> p(mu,sigma*) = p(mu*,sigma)
>      >>
>      >> We know this because of continuity and that p(mu,sigma) is bounded
>      >> between 0 and p(mu*,sigma*).
>      >>
>      >> So how do I really define identifiability?
>      >>
>      >> Also, is it kosher to use the term "weakly identifiable" for one
>      >> of those normal(0,gazillion) priors?
>      >>
>      >> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] rstan memory use
messages.body_plain:
What we really need is a format to save fits that portable
across CmdStan/RStan/PyStan and doesn't involve any R at all!
We're moving in that direction, and will hopefully work something
out at some point this year (not a very encouraging time frame,
but it is on our medium-term to-do list).

Having said that, I have no idea whether the environments are
there for a reason in R or not.

- Bob

On 2/8/14, 2:32 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> A lot of the memory rstan's fit objects use is sneaking in through the back door.
>
> I have one fit object that is about 488Mb when saved to disk with save().  The .Misc object (one of the slots), which is
> an environment, occupies 435Mb of that.  The environment itself has only one item, which doesn't look too big.  So I
> assume what is happening is that the enclosing environment, and its enclosing environment, and so on are getting saved
> as well.
>
> My understanding is that environments are shared objects, so that multiple objects referencing the same environment see
> the same thing, and do not create copies.  Also, at least some environments (maybe the base and global environments) are
> not saved to disk.  I'm not sure if package environments (imports:rstan is toward the top of the enclosing environment
> frames for .Misc) are saved, or simply an indication to load the appropriate library (since I've noticed that load() can
> trigger messages that libraries are being loaded).
>
> My typical usage involves saving fit objects to disk and then reading them into other processes.  I suspect that this
> breaks the sharing of environments, that is a I get one new copy with each object read in.
>
> I don't know if there's anything that can be done about this, but if there's a way to avoid it that would be nice.
>
> I discovered this because I've been running simulations with multiple fit objects, and my jobs require a lot of memory,
> like 16GB.  I have also been sending some objects between processes (with Rmpi). environments crop up in a lot of
> unexpected (to me) places: every formula has one, and so does a model frame.  And so does a stanfit object.  So, for
> example, I have one formula that required 3.5G to save to disk; it was a couple hundred bytes after I replaced the
> environment with one of the canonical ones like emptyenv() or baseenv().  I later discovered empytenv() was a poor
> choice since it causes operations on the formula to fail with messages like "can't find list function".
>
> Ross Boylan
>

messages.body_plain:
Got it!    And it's a good lesson in exception handling.

If you look at:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/commit/ce0d4157aa0a214c3830a9ac7057f1156276b954

you'll see that

  try {
    z.V = - stan::model::log_prob_grad<true,true>(_model, z.q, z.g, _err_stream);
  } catch (std::domain_error e) {
    this->_write_error_msg(_err_stream, e);
    z.V = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();
  }

was replaced with

   try {
     stan::model::gradient<true, true>(_model, z.q, z.V, z.g, _err_stream);
   } catch (std::domain_error e) {
     this->_write_error_msg(_err_stream, e);
     z.V = std::numeric_limits<double>::infinity();
   }
   z.V *= -1;

The z.V *= -1 should have gone inside the try, not outside.
That is, it should only get called when the gradient there succeeded.

I'll create an issue, fix it on a branch and create a pull request
ASAP.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "identifiability" is a tricky concept
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I'll probably just blog my remarks on identifiability along with Ben's updates.

Bob:  regarding your chapter:  I think it has some good things in it but I also think it's too theoretical for the Stan manual and also has excursions into maximum likelihood that will be more confusing than helpful to readers.  I'd just get rid of section 19.1 and keep the rest.

There's also a larger question of how much of this sort of thing belongs in the manual at all.  It seems to be a better fit for our future book!  I guess it's ok to park it in the manual for now, but once we do the book it might make sense to take this material out of the manual.

A

On Feb 8, 2014, at 2:36 AM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> I just took a whack at writing up a chapter on identifiability
> for the manual, but realize I may have gotten in over my head
> philosophically.  I've attached the draft chapter (for some
> reason, printing to pdf in Mac OS preview changed the page size).
>
> I bcc-ed Richard McElreath, who originally inspired this endeavour
> with his question to stan-users (Richard, you can reply to me at
> ca...@alias-i.com or respond on the users list).
>
> The issue comes up fairly often on the users list, so it seems worth
> saying something.   It brings up lots of good issues with how
> sampling works.
>
> Feel free to grab the branch
>
>  feature/issue-485-next-manual
>
> and update or send me comments (as long as they're not too complex
> for me to understand) and I'll update.
>
> Now we just need to get Andrew's friend to turn it all into
> a blog post and then a paper :-)
>
> - Bob
>
> On 2/8/14, 1:52 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> On Thursday, February 6, 2014 10:48:48 AM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>>
>>    Identification is actually a tricky concept and is not so clearly defined.
>>
>>
>> I agree that a lot of people use the word identification without defining what they mean, but there are no shortage of
>> definitions out there. However, I'm not sure that identification is that helpful a concept for the practical problems we
>> are trying to solve here when providing recommendations on how users should write .stan files.
>>
>> I think many if not most people that think about identification rigorously have in mind a concept that is
>> pre-statistical. So, for them it is going to sound weird to associate "identification" with problems that arise with a
>> particular sample or a particular computational approach. In economics, the idea of identification of a parameter goes
>> back at least to the Cowles Commission guys, such as in the first couple of papers here
>>
>> http://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&q=author%3ATC-Koopmans+identification&btnG=&as_sdt=1%2C33
>>
>> In causal inference, the idea of identification of an average causal effect is a property of a DAG in Pearl's stuff
>>
>> http://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/jp_home.html
>>
>>    In the broadest sense, a Bayesian model is identified if the posterior distribution is proper.  Then one can do
>>    Bayesian inference and that's that.  No need to require a finite variance or even a finite mean, all that's needed
>>    is a finite integral of the probability distribution.
>>
>>
>> I don't disagree, but what good is the word "identified"? If the posterior distribution is improper, then there is no
>> Bayesian inference.
>>
>>    That said, there are some reasons why a stronger definition can be useful:
>>
>>    1.  Weak identification.  Suppose that, with reasonable data, you'd have a posterior with a sd of 1 (or that order
>>    of magnitude).  But you have sparse data or collinearity or whatever, and so you have some dimension in your
>>    posterior that's really flat, some "ridge" with a sd of 1000.  Then it makes sense to say that this parameter or
>>    linear combination of parameters is only weakly identified.  Or one can say that it's identified from the prior but
>>    not the likelihood.
>>
>>
>> Here again we are running into the problem of other people associating the phrase "weak identification" with a different
>> thing (usually instrumental variable models where the instruments are weak predictors of the variable they are
>> instrumenting for). This paper
>>
>> http://cowles.econ.yale.edu/~dwka/pub/p1370.pdf
>>
>> basically is interested in situations where some parameter is not identified iff another parameter is zero. And then
>> they drift the population toward that zero.
>>
>>    So, yes, Bob, as chief rabbi I say it is kosher to refer to weak identifiability.  If we wanted to make the concept
>>    more formal, we'd stipulate that the model is expressed in terms of some hyperparameter A which is set to a large
>>    value, and that weak identifiability corresponds to nonidentifiability when A -> infinity.
>>
>>
>> If we were going to go this route, then it is good to be specific with the definitions but I still don't know if you
>> want to call this situation "weak identifiability".
>>
>>    Even there, though, some tricky cases arise.  For example, suppose your model includes a parameter p that is defined
>>    on [0,1] and is given a flat prior, and suppose the data don't tell us anything about p, so that our posterior is
>>    also U(0,1).  That sounds nonidentified to me, but it does have a finite integral.
>>
>>
>> Do you mean that a particular sample doesn't tell us anything about p or that data are incapable of telling us anything
>> about p? In addition, I think it is helpful to distinguish between situations where
>>
>> 1. There is a unique maximum likelihood estimator (perhaps with probability 1)
>> 2. There is not a unique maximum likelihood estimator but the likelihood is not flat everywhere with respect to a
>>    parameter proposal
>> 3. The likelihood is flat everywhere with respect to a parameter proposal
>>
>> What bothers me about some notion of "computational identifiability" is that a Stan user may be in situation 1 but
>> through some combination of weird priors, bad starting values, too few iterations, finite-precision, particular choice
>> of metric, maladaptation, and / or bad luck can't get one or more chains to converge to the stationary distribution of
>> the parameters. That's a practical problem that Stan users face, but I don't think many people would consider it to be
>> an identification problem.
>>
>> Maybe something that is somewhat unique to Stan is the idea of identified in the constrained parameter space but not
>> identified in the unconstrained parameter space like we have with uniform sampling on the unit sphere.
>>
>>    2.  Aliasing.  Consider an item response model or mixture model where the direction or labeling is unspecified.
>>      Then you can have 2 or 4 or K! different reflections of the posterior.  Even if all priors are proper, so the full
>>    posterior is proper, it contains all these copies so this labeling is not identified in any real sense.
>>
>>
>> This one doesn't bother me as much because you can at least conceptually restrict the parameter space to preclude all
>> but one of the reflections, although whether it is easy to do that in Stan is another matter.
>>
>>    Here, and in general, identification depends not just on the model but also on the data.  So, strictly speaking, one
>>    should not talk about an "identifiable model" but rather an 'identifiable fitted model" or "identifiable parameters"
>>    within a fitted model.
>>
>>
>> Certainly, whether you have computational problems depends on the data, among other things. But to say that
>> identification depends on the data goes against the conventional usage where identification is pre-statistical so we
>> need to think about whether it would be more effective to try to redefine identification or to use other phrases to
>> describe the problems we are trying to overcome.
>>
>> Ben
>>
>>    On Feb 6, 2014, at 12:46 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>
>>     > I think you're misreading the definitions.  Remember, classical identifiably
>>     > is in the regime of classical statistics, which means likelihoods!
>>     >
>>     > Identifiability on Wikipedia is defined such that if two likelihood _distributions_
>>     > (i.e. we haven't measured the data yet) are distinct then the parameters
>>     > labeling them are distinct.  This means that, provided you measure
>>     > enough data, you will be able to discriminate between the two
>>     > likelihood distributions (and hence the parameters that label them).
>>     >
>>     > This is not the same as the likelihood _values_ being equal for a given
>>     > data set.  Remember, "ensembles of possible data sets" not
>>     > "the actual data set that I fricken measured".
>>     >
>>     > A more intuitive (and I believe equivalent) definition is that in the limit
>>     > of infinite data the MLE will converge to a single value equal to the
>>     > true parameters.  Multimodality?  Unidentified.  The y ~ N(mu1 + m2, sigma)
>>     > example?  Unidentified both with and without a proper prior.
>>     >
>>     > The big difference in Bayesian modeling is that we're conditioning
>>     > on only the measured data so the infinite data limit isn't as meaningful.
>>     > Uncertainty is fine so long as it's finite.  So I tend to think of a parameter
>>     > as being identified if its marginal variance is finite, even if it doesn't
>>     > vanish as the data expands towards infinity.
>>     >
>>     >> From this perspective we can think of identifiability as a spectrum,
>>     > from weak (large marginal variance as the data grows) to strong
>>     > (small, possibly vanishing marginal variance as as the data grows).
>>     >
>>     > On Feb 5, 2014, at 11:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <javascript:>> wrote:
>>     >
>>     >> It doesn't look to me like the usual notion of identifiability is right,
>>     >> at least not in a Bayesian setting.  Both Greene's book where I just read
>>     >> this and the Wikipedia define identifiability as
>>     >>
>>     >>  theta != theta'  if and only if   p(theta) != p(theta')
>>     >>
>>     >> That is, the probability function is one-to-one.
>>     >>
>>     >> But that can't be right.  If we have parameters mu and sigma for a normal
>>     >> model with some data y, then let mu* and sigma* be the MLE.
>>     >>
>>     >> Then if mu != mu*, there must be some sigma != sigma* such that
>>     >>
>>     >> p(mu,sigma*) = p(mu*,sigma)
>>     >>
>>     >> We know this because of continuity and that p(mu,sigma) is bounded
>>     >> between 0 and p(mu*,sigma*).
>>     >>
>>     >> So how do I really define identifiability?
>>     >>
>>     >> Also, is it kosher to use the term "weakly identifiable" for one
>>     >> of those normal(0,gazillion) priors?
>>     >>
>>     >> - Bob
>>     >>

messages.body_plain:
On 2/8/14, 11:06 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi all.  I'll probably just blog my remarks on identifiability along with Ben's updates.

I figured it'd be too tempting to resist.

> Bob:  regarding your chapter:  I think it has some good things in it but I also think it's too theoretical for the Stan manual and also has excursions into maximum likelihood that will be more confusing than helpful to readers.  I'd just get rid of section 19.1 and keep the rest.

The Stan manual bounces around a lot in its level of theory (which
is not really a good thing, because it's not layered in any natural
way).  I think  that's partly because I've been using it partly to
clarify my own understanding of these issues.

Stan already provides MLE, so it's not really stepping outside of
what Stan does!  I could make that connection clearer.

I find without the MLE definitions, the whole concept is too vague.

How strongly do you feel about getting rid of 19.1?  If you feel
strongly about it, I'll drop it in favor of a vague allusion to
non-Bayesian concepts of identifiability.

I do feel that when you talked about a U(0,1) not being identified,
it was this MLE notion speaking.

> There's also a larger question of how much of this sort of thing belongs in
 > the manual at all.  It seems to be a better fit for our future book!  I guess it's
 > ok to park it in the manual for now, but once we do the book it might make sense
 > to take this material out of the manual.

I also write in the manual rather than doing hard work, like debugging.
You can think of it like a blog that just keeps growing :-)

Seriously, though, the identifiability issue comes up again and again and
we need to give our users at least some concrete advice and also I think
it helps to give them some feeling for what's going on with HMC, which is
unfamiliar to a lot of them who are well versed in Gibbs.

I think of the manual as coming in two parts.  The first part is the
user's programming guide and the second part is the actual language spec.
I put this in the first half, because it's not part of the language or
implementation itself.

Then there's all the stuff that doesn't really fit anywhere like the
intro to MCMC.

- Bob

> A
>

>
>> I just took a whack at writing up a chapter on identifiability
>> for the manual, but realize I may have gotten in over my head
>> philosophically.  I've attached the draft chapter (for some
>> reason, printing to pdf in Mac OS preview changed the page size).

>> a blog post and then a paper :-)
>>
>> - Bob

>> On 2/8/14, 1:52 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>>> On Thursday, February 6, 2014 10:48:48 AM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>>>
>>>     Identification is actually a tricky concept and is not so clearly defined.
>>>
>>>
>>> I agree that a lot of people use the word identification without defining what they mean, but there are no shortage of
>>> definitions out there. However, I'm not sure that identification is that helpful a concept for the practical problems we
>>> are trying to solve here when providing recommendations on how users should write .stan files.
>>>
>>> I think many if not most people that think about identification rigorously have in mind a concept that is
>>> pre-statistical. So, for them it is going to sound weird to associate "identification" with problems that arise with a
>>> particular sample or a particular computational approach. In economics, the idea of identification of a parameter goes
>>> back at least to the Cowles Commission guys, such as in the first couple of papers here
>>>
>>> http://scholar.google.com/scholar?hl=en&q=author%3ATC-Koopmans+identification&btnG=&as_sdt=1%2C33
>>>
>>> In causal inference, the idea of identification of an average causal effect is a property of a DAG in Pearl's stuff
>>>
>>> http://bayes.cs.ucla.edu/jp_home.html
>>>
>>>     In the broadest sense, a Bayesian model is identified if the posterior distribution is proper.  Then one can do
>>>     Bayesian inference and that's that.  No need to require a finite variance or even a finite mean, all that's needed
>>>     is a finite integral of the probability distribution.
>>>
>>>
>>> I don't disagree, but what good is the word "identified"? If the posterior distribution is improper, then there is no
>>> Bayesian inference.
>>>
>>>     That said, there are some reasons why a stronger definition can be useful:
>>>
>>>     1.  Weak identification.  Suppose that, with reasonable data, you'd have a posterior with a sd of 1 (or that order
>>>     of magnitude).  But you have sparse data or collinearity or whatever, and so you have some dimension in your
>>>     posterior that's really flat, some "ridge" with a sd of 1000.  Then it makes sense to say that this parameter or
>>>     linear combination of parameters is only weakly identified.  Or one can say that it's identified from the prior but
>>>     not the likelihood.
>>>
>>>
>>> Here again we are running into the problem of other people associating the phrase "weak identification" with a different
>>> thing (usually instrumental variable models where the instruments are weak predictors of the variable they are
>>> instrumenting for). This paper
>>>
>>> http://cowles.econ.yale.edu/~dwka/pub/p1370.pdf
>>>
>>> basically is interested in situations where some parameter is not identified iff another parameter is zero. And then
>>> they drift the population toward that zero.
>>>
>>>     So, yes, Bob, as chief rabbi I say it is kosher to refer to weak identifiability.  If we wanted to make the concept
>>>     more formal, we'd stipulate that the model is expressed in terms of some hyperparameter A which is set to a large
>>>     value, and that weak identifiability corresponds to nonidentifiability when A -> infinity.
>>>
>>>
>>> If we were going to go this route, then it is good to be specific with the definitions but I still don't know if you
>>> want to call this situation "weak identifiability".
>>>
>>>     Even there, though, some tricky cases arise.  For example, suppose your model includes a parameter p that is defined
>>>     on [0,1] and is given a flat prior, and suppose the data don't tell us anything about p, so that our posterior is
>>>     also U(0,1).  That sounds nonidentified to me, but it does have a finite integral.
>>>
>>>
>>> Do you mean that a particular sample doesn't tell us anything about p or that data are incapable of telling us anything
>>> about p? In addition, I think it is helpful to distinguish between situations where
>>>
>>> 1. There is a unique maximum likelihood estimator (perhaps with probability 1)
>>> 2. There is not a unique maximum likelihood estimator but the likelihood is not flat everywhere with respect to a
>>>     parameter proposal
>>> 3. The likelihood is flat everywhere with respect to a parameter proposal
>>>
>>> What bothers me about some notion of "computational identifiability" is that a Stan user may be in situation 1 but
>>> through some combination of weird priors, bad starting values, too few iterations, finite-precision, particular choice
>>> of metric, maladaptation, and / or bad luck can't get one or more chains to converge to the stationary distribution of
>>> the parameters. That's a practical problem that Stan users face, but I don't think many people would consider it to be
>>> an identification problem.
>>>
>>> Maybe something that is somewhat unique to Stan is the idea of identified in the constrained parameter space but not
>>> identified in the unconstrained parameter space like we have with uniform sampling on the unit sphere.
>>>
>>>     2.  Aliasing.  Consider an item response model or mixture model where the direction or labeling is unspecified.
>>>       Then you can have 2 or 4 or K! different reflections of the posterior.  Even if all priors are proper, so the full
>>>     posterior is proper, it contains all these copies so this labeling is not identified in any real sense.
>>>
>>>
>>> This one doesn't bother me as much because you can at least conceptually restrict the parameter space to preclude all
>>> but one of the reflections, although whether it is easy to do that in Stan is another matter.
>>>
>>>     Here, and in general, identification depends not just on the model but also on the data.  So, strictly speaking, one
>>>     should not talk about an "identifiable model" but rather an 'identifiable fitted model" or "identifiable parameters"
>>>     within a fitted model.
>>>
>>>
>>> Certainly, whether you have computational problems depends on the data, among other things. But to say that
>>> identification depends on the data goes against the conventional usage where identification is pre-statistical so we
>>> need to think about whether it would be more effective to try to redefine identification or to use other phrases to
>>> describe the problems we are trying to overcome.
>>>
>>> Ben
>>>
>>>     On Feb 6, 2014, at 12:46 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>>>
>>>      > I think you're misreading the definitions.  Remember, classical identifiably
>>>      > is in the regime of classical statistics, which means likelihoods!
>>>      >
>>>      > Identifiability on Wikipedia is defined such that if two likelihood _distributions_
>>>      > (i.e. we haven't measured the data yet) are distinct then the parameters
>>>      > labeling them are distinct.  This means that, provided you measure
>>>      > enough data, you will be able to discriminate between the two
>>>      > likelihood distributions (and hence the parameters that label them).
>>>      >
>>>      > This is not the same as the likelihood _values_ being equal for a given
>>>      > data set.  Remember, "ensembles of possible data sets" not
>>>      > "the actual data set that I fricken measured".
>>>      >
>>>      > A more intuitive (and I believe equivalent) definition is that in the limit
>>>      > of infinite data the MLE will converge to a single value equal to the
>>>      > true parameters.  Multimodality?  Unidentified.  The y ~ N(mu1 + m2, sigma)
>>>      > example?  Unidentified both with and without a proper prior.
>>>      >
>>>      > The big difference in Bayesian modeling is that we're conditioning
>>>      > on only the measured data so the infinite data limit isn't as meaningful.
>>>      > Uncertainty is fine so long as it's finite.  So I tend to think of a parameter
>>>      > as being identified if its marginal variance is finite, even if it doesn't
>>>      > vanish as the data expands towards infinity.
>>>      >
>>>      >> From this perspective we can think of identifiability as a spectrum,
>>>      > from weak (large marginal variance as the data grows) to strong
>>>      > (small, possibly vanishing marginal variance as as the data grows).
>>>      >
>>>      > On Feb 5, 2014, at 11:28 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <javascript:>> wrote:
>>>      >
>>>      >> It doesn't look to me like the usual notion of identifiability is right,
>>>      >> at least not in a Bayesian setting.  Both Greene's book where I just read
>>>      >> this and the Wikipedia define identifiability as
>>>      >>
>>>      >>  theta != theta'  if and only if   p(theta) != p(theta')
>>>      >>
>>>      >> That is, the probability function is one-to-one.
>>>      >>
>>>      >> But that can't be right.  If we have parameters mu and sigma for a normal
>>>      >> model with some data y, then let mu* and sigma* be the MLE.
>>>      >>
>>>      >> Then if mu != mu*, there must be some sigma != sigma* such that
>>>      >>
>>>      >> p(mu,sigma*) = p(mu*,sigma)
>>>      >>
>>>      >> We know this because of continuity and that p(mu,sigma) is bounded
>>>      >> between 0 and p(mu*,sigma*).
>>>      >>
>>>      >> So how do I really define identifiability?
>>>      >>
>>>      >> Also, is it kosher to use the term "weakly identifiable" for one
>>>      >> of those normal(0,gazillion) priors?
>>>      >>
>>>      >> - Bob

This part seems to have a logical problem:

"Model identifiability is a necessary (but not sufficient) condition for the existence of maximum likelihood estimates (MLE). Without identifiability, the maximum likelihood estimate might not be unique."

If it's a necessary condition, how does the MLE might not be unique? (if, so it should never exist/be unique)

Btw, nice chapter and nice topic, I'm really learning a lot.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] "identifiability" is a tricky concept
messages.body_plain:
I think you should start with 19.4 and avoid the word identifiability. The basic question you are trying to address is "What are the situations where the posterior is proper, but Stan nevertheless has trouble sampling from that posterior?" There is not much to say about improper posteriors, except that you basically can't do Bayesian inference. Although Stan can optimize a log-likelihood function, everybody doing so should know that you can't do maximum likelihood inference without a unique maximum. Then, there are a few things that are problematic such as long ridges, multiple modes (even if they are not exactly the same height), label switches and reflections, densities that approach infinity at some point(s), densities that are not differentiable, discontinuities, integerizing a continuous variable, good in the constrained space vs. bad in the constrained space, etc. And then we can suggest what to do about each of these specific things without trying to squeeze them under the umbrella of identifiability.

Ben

messages.subject: breaking apart manual + Stan book?
messages.body_plain:
I think we should step back and ask ourselves who we think
our target audience is and what we're trying to help them do.

As is, the manual's trying to serve (at least) the following
four different purposes.

I'd be happy to take responsibility for the first two of these
and leave the third and fourth to others.  I think a "Stan Book"
would most naturally serve the third and maybe the fourth purpose.

Stan Reference
--------------

   Part IV   Modeling Language Reference
   Part V    Built-in Functions
   Part VI   Discrete Distributions
   Part VII  Continuous Distributions

   Chapter 51  Transformations of Variables

   Appendix D.  Stan Program Style Guide

CmdStan Reference
-----------------

   Part II Commands and Data Formats

   Appendix A  Licensing

   Appendix B  Installation and Compatibility

Intro to Stan Modeling
----------------------------------------

   Chapter 2  Getting Started

   Part III  Programming Techniques

   Appendix C.  Stan for Users of BUGS

Intro to (Computational) (Bayesian) Stats
---------------------------------------

   Chapter 48.  (Penalized) MLE and Posterior Modes (I was just writing this)

   Chapter 49.  Bayesian Data Analysis

   Cahpter 50.  MCMC

   Chapter 19.  Identifiability

- Bob

On 2/9/14, 11:38 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> I agree.  Although it could be useful to mention the term "identifiability" just to say that this is a related concept.

Andrew followed his own advice in BDA, but it never gets defined,
which is why I think I was so confused about what it meant.  Because
the usage in BDA is not the usual notion from non-Bayesian stats.

In ARM, Gelman and Hill (p. 220) are more precise, saying

    Identifiability refers to whether the data contain sufficient information
    for unique estimation of a given parameter or set of parameters in a particular
    model.

The cases mentioned in BDA and arm are (a) collinearity in regressions, (b)
separability in logistic regressions, (c) additive and multiplicative nonidentifiability
in IRT-like models, and (d) mixture model "label switching".

This is obviously not the usual definition of identifiability for MLE
(as defined in Greene and on the Wikipedia) and presumably why Andrew
didn't like my first section --- it doesn't match his usage of the term.

So I propose I just drop this notion of "identifiability" altogether and
concentrate on "problematic posteriors".

More below on what I think that should entail.

> On Feb 9, 2014, at 11:35 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

...

>> There is not much to say about improper posteriors, except that you basically can't do Bayesian inference.

I disagree.  The problem stems from advice from Andrew and others
in the context of Gibbs.  Advice our users are trying to apply to Stan,
with no luck, leading them to conclude Stan is slow.

Check out ARM's section 19.4, "Redundant parameters and intentionally nonidentifiable
models".  Here Andrew and Jennifer suggest for computational efficiency to use
parameterizations that are not identifiable and then post-process to something that is.

This works fine in Gibbs for reasons I tried to explain in the section Ben wants
me to cut, but won't work in Stan for reasons I try to explain in the same section.

>> Although Stan can optimize a log-likelihood function, everybody doing so should
 >> know that you can't do maximum
>> likelihood inference without a unique maximum.

"Should know" and "do know" can be miles apart.

But I think the bigger point is that people try to do inference all the
time when parameters aren't identified in the sense of Gelman and Hill.
Sometimes the models aren't identified in the sense of Greene and the
Wikipedia and sometimes they are.

For example, in the two-location parameter example I was going to include,
you get perfectly reasonable predictions for new data with any of the
maximal (not maximum) likelihood estimates --- just as good
as with the single parameter model.  You also get reasonable inferences in
Gibbs and even in Stan.  It's just that your paramters aren't
identified in the Gelman/Hill sense.

Same thing with collinear predictors under L1 priors --- the
model plus data don't give a unique MLE, but the inferences are just fine in
most cases because most software takes finitely many finite steps.

- Bob

Take it up with Andrew and Jennifer :-)

Seriously, though, what I meant was that if you sample
something like:

   y ~ normal(lambda1 + lambda2, sigma);

then mu = (lambda1 + lambda2) is going to be well behaved
in that it'll take on the same value as mu would if you'd
just written

   y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Each update of lambda conditioned on lambda2 and sigma is
very constrained.

Sure, if you ran forever you might run into floating point
problems.

up for lambda1 + lambda2.

I am NOT suggesting that users do this for Stan, just that
the reason they think it's working in Gibbs is because of
the correlation between lambda1 and lambda2 in the posterior
and Gibbs's slow exploration of it.

- Bob

Absolutely not "UI" or "UX" as that seems to imply GUI.

I'm in favor of stan_api.

We should talk about this split at the next meeting.  I've
been talking to Mitzi about I/O formats.  JSON's rather heavy,
even compared to CSV, and the spec's rather loose in the HTML
tradition, with language like "SHOULD" [which is defined in another
RFC!] for things like uniqueness of keys in their equivalent of
maps/associative-arrays.

Also, the Boost tools to parse it are lacking in SAX-like parsers,
though other ones exist.

On Fri, Feb 14, 2014 at 4:46 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

>
>
> On 2/14/14, 10:33 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > CmdStan feels like a "GUI" to me... and that's why you shouldn't have me designing interfaces.
>
> Right!  CmdStan is the UI, not the C++ code that it calls.
>
> Could you remind me again of what's going into this "ui" namespace.
> I'd think most of it should either go into MCMC or into an optimization
> namespace if we don't already have one.

It's going to include:
- print methods.
  We have lots of different print methods right now. The function that prints something like "Iteration: 0 / 10 [  0%]  (Warmup)" should go in here if we want it to be displayed consistently across all our interfaces. So far, we have functions for: do_print (the logic to determine whether to print), print_progress, write_error_msg, write_iteration and write_iteration_csv (used for optimization only -- should rename at some point), write_model (writes the name of the model), and write_stan (writes out the Stan version number).
- MCMC / optmization logic
  I think this is what you're thinking of. For example, the logic to call any particular sampler should be shared across all interfaces. Perhaps that belongs in the mcmc or optimization namespace, but right now, all the logic is sitting in a monster 747-line function called command(). What's in src/stan/gm/command.hpp is really a CmdStan specific command() function. RStan and PyStan both duplicate most of the code to do the logic, which is why it's hard keeping things in synch. I think part of the reason is the data formats and streams. I'm hoping we can get the bulk of the logic in interface agnostic code that can be called by {Cmd,R,Py}Stan where each of the interfaces will just have a thin wrapper around the common functions.

If you want to see the duplication of code, compare RStan's stan_fit.hpp to PyStan's stan stan_fit.hpp to Stan's command.hpp. Links below:
Stan: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/stan/gm/command.hpp
RStan: https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/blob/develop/rstan/rstan/inst/include/rstan/stan_fit.hpp
PyStan: https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan/blob/develop/pystan/stan_fit.hpp

I don't plan on letting Jiqiang and Allen suffer with theses changes alone. I think I can help update Stan + the 3 interfaces. First Stan + CmdStan (until we can split it out), then RStan and PyStan.

Things that need to be broken out:
- gm/arguments/**.
  All the argument stuff is CmdStan specific. Unless we use that as a representation of the arguments across the interfaces. I don't think it's quite ready to be used in that way right now. We can beef it up so it can be used in that manner.
- CmdStan: command line specific calls
  So we'd need to wrap the reusable logic in ui or wherever and feed it the appropriate streams. We need to start giving it equal status as RStan and PyStan instead of treating it as the reference implementation. Whatever we consider "reference" should go into the shared logic and hopefully that'll allow us to update all interfaces really easily.

> The rest, that's not going to be used by RStan or PyStan, can go
> into something like "stan::command".  Or if we want to break that out,
> "stan::command::summary" for what's bin/print, "stan::command::fit" for
> what's now a compiled model or just command.  And so on.

Yeah, I want to start prepping us to break out CmdStan into its own repository. In RStan, Stan is a git submodule. In PyStan, there's a copy of Stan that's in the repository. For CmdStan, I think we want to go with the git submodule route. Although there's some overhead for the developer in keeping it in synch, there's added flexibility in being able to work with non-tagged versions of Stan easily.

>
>
> > Although, these are the building blocks for a UI, which was why I was thinking 'ui' or 'ux.' But I'm perfectly happy
> > calling it stan_api.
> >
> > I'll give it a few days for the dust to settle before locking in any decision.
>
> All locks are breakable. :-)

=). Yeah they are.

I feel a lot more confident about these changes having seen the implementations for RStan and PyStan. Oh yeah, refactoring C++ is a pain in the ass. And I'm adding more tests as I go along.

Daniel

> - print methods.

>   We have lots of different print methods right now. The function that prints something like "Iteration: 0 / 10 [  0%]  (Warmup)" should go in here if we want it to be displayed consistently across all our interfaces. So far, we have functions for: do_print (the logic to determine whether to print), print_progress, write_error_msg, write_iteration and write_iteration_csv (used for optimization only -- should rename at some point), write_model (writes the name of the model), and write_stan (writes out the Stan version number).

I think what we need here is a base writer and then derived writers for each method that specify
the outputs for those methods.  The iteration message you noted above would belong to the
sample_writer (change the name of the mcmc_writer to align with the method names).

This would also require a decision on how to pass along streams internally.

> - MCMC / optmization logic
>   I think this is what you're thinking of. For example, the logic to call any particular sampler should be shared across all interfaces. Perhaps that belongs in the mcmc or optimization namespace, but right now, all the logic is sitting in a monster 747-line function called command(). What's in src/stan/gm/command.hpp is really a CmdStan specific command() function. RStan and PyStan both duplicate most of the code to do the logic, which is why it's hard keeping things in synch. I think part of the reason is the data formats and streams. I'm hoping we can get the bulk of the logic in interface agnostic code that can be called by {Cmd,R,Py}Stan where each of the interfaces will just have a thin wrapper around the common functions.
>
> If you want to see the duplication of code, compare RStan's stan_fit.hpp to PyStan's stan stan_fit.hpp to Stan's command.hpp. Links below:
> Stan: https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/stan/gm/command.hpp
> RStan: https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/blob/develop/rstan/rstan/inst/include/rstan/stan_fit.hpp
> PyStan: https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan/blob/develop/pystan/stan_fit.hpp
>
> I don't plan on letting Jiqiang and Allen suffer with theses changes alone. I think I can help update Stan + the 3 interfaces. First Stan + CmdStan (until we can split it out), then RStan and PyStan.

Right.  All the samplers should have to do is specify a configuration and provide input streams or contexts (data, inits, etc) and output streams
(output, diagnostics, etc).

> Things that need to be broken out:
> - gm/arguments/**.
>   All the argument stuff is CmdStan specific. Unless we use that as a representation of the arguments across the interfaces. I don't think it's quite ready to be used in that way right now. We can beef it up so it can be used in that manner.

Agreed.  The big issue is moving from file names to explicit I/O objects.  I’m not sure how robust the
var_context is — what we really need is some object that provides the input data and some object
that accepts the output data.  Then each interface is responsible for constructing these objects
and passing them to the API.

In short, I think the biggest priorities are
1) Defining internal I/O objects and specs.
2) Refactoring the optimizers so that they’re modular like the samplers.
3) Split up command into separate functions taking in the configuration as an arguments.

> This would also require a decision on how to pass along streams internally.

The question is whether it even needs to be streams!  If we had a GUI, it
wouldn't be streams.

The more general thing to do would be to invoke callbacks that got handled
however the interface wanted to deal with them.  One way it could deal is
by formatting and writing to a stream.

This may be overkill at this point, though.

>> - MCMC / optmization logic
>>   I think this is what you're thinking of. For example, the logic to call any particular sampler should be shared
>> across all interfaces. Perhaps that belongs in the mcmc or optimization namespace, but right now, all the logic is
>> sitting in a monster 747-line function called command(). What's in src/stan/gm/command.hpp is really a CmdStan
>> specific command() function. RStan and PyStan both duplicate most of the code to do the logic, which is why it's hard
>> keeping things in synch. I think part of the reason is the data formats and streams. I'm hoping we can get the bulk of
>> the logic in interface agnostic code that can be called by {Cmd,R,Py}Stan where each of the interfaces will just have
>> a thin wrapper around the common functions.
>>

>> command.hpp. Links below:

>> PyStan: https://github.com/stan-dev/pystan/blob/develop/pystan/stan_fit.hpp
>>
>> I don't plan on letting Jiqiang and Allen suffer with theses changes alone. I think I can help update Stan + the 3
>> interfaces. First Stan + CmdStan (until we can split it out), then RStan and PyStan.
>
> Right.  All the samplers should have to do is specify a configuration and provide input streams or contexts (data,
> inits, etc) and output streams
> (output, diagnostics, etc).

I think we're all agreed here.  We need output contexts, as well.
RStan doesn't write to a file, it writes to R's memory.  Presumably
PyStan does the same thing with Python.

So I think we need something like var_context for output.  More below
on what I think we need.

>> Things that need to be broken out:
>> - gm/arguments/**.
>>   All the argument stuff is CmdStan specific. Unless we use that as a representation of the arguments across the
>> interfaces. I don't think it's quite ready to be used in that way right now. We can beef it up so it can be used in
>> that manner.
>
> Agreed.  The big issue is moving from file names to explicit I/O objects.  I’m not sure how robust the
> var_context is —

Robust in what sense?   The code's not very general or well written.
I think the basic idea of the design is right --- you want an object
that can instantiated with a file or through R's memory or Python's memory
that gives the sampler a way to read data so it can populate the member
variables of a model.  Same for initial values.  And when we allow mass
matrices to be read in, same for that, too.

> what we really need is some object that provides the input data and some object
> that accepts the output data.  Then each interface is responsible for constructing these objects
> and passing them to the API.

Exactly.

The big question in my mind is whether the output object acts like an
output or whether it buffers and acts like an input.  Output is most
efficient and we could always wrap it in a buffer.

> In short, I think the biggest priorities are
> 1) Defining internal I/O objects and specs.

I think we need something like var_context for input, and we could use
it for:

a.  data reads in models
b.  initialization reads for samplers or optimizers
c.  initialization reads for mass matrices + step size

and perhaps

d.  initialization read for configurations.

I add (d) because I think we may want the structure of the config to
look similar to everything else, only be structured like a properties
object (associative array) as in JSON.

I've been looking at JSON today, and it's damn heavy itself and
based on string representations.  The idea is that we want something
programmatic rather than based on a file format.

That's what I was trying to do with var_context, which is currently
being used for (a) and (b) and could be pressed into duty for (c).

For output, we have complementary needs:

i.   output of configuration
ii.  output of mass matrices
iii.  output of warmup iterations and post-warmup draws

Ideally these would all make it easy to round-trip.  I've been thinking
about this in the context of posterior predictive checks, where we want
to be able to take draws from the posterior (now a row in the CSV output
linked to the header in CmdStan) and use them as input for a new model (now in R dump
format in CmdStan).  RStan's better behaved here, I think.

We also need to be abel to take the last draw and use it to initialize
a new chain.  And be able to take the adapted mass matrix and step size
and use it to configure a new chain ---- this can be used to either throw
out the current draws post-warmup and resample or to continue from where
we left off in sampling.

> 2) Refactoring the optimizers so that they’re modular like the samplers.
> 3) Split up command into separate functions taking in the configuration as an arguments.

Agreed and agreed.

- Bob

messages.subject: encapsulating install in RStan?
messages.body_plain:
I'd like to try to cut down on the wave of install problems that
are getting reported lately (which may just indicate more users
and may all be Rcpp 0.11.0 related).  Here's what I think we can do:

1.  *Encapsulate instructions per platform.*

I want to write instructions on a per-platform basis rather
than as a series of steps and instructions like we have now.  I
can do that, but Daniel needs to send me the login info for Andrew's
office machine and some hints at how to access its desktop remotely.

2.  *Encapsulate our install*

I would like to investigate ways to encapsulate our install
as much as possible.  The steps I'd like to take are:

2a.  Isolate from user's R config.

Ben mentioned during the meeting that there might be a way to
guarantee that our own Makevars gets used (or if we don't need that,
at least that the system-wide and user-specific one don't get in the
way).  What are the steps to do that?

2b.  Fix a particular Rcpp version.

Is there a way to use a version of Rcpp other than the most recent
without interfering with the rest of the user's environment?  If so,
I'd like to freeze Rcpp versions until we know more recent ones work.

2c.  Fix a particular C++ toolchain.

I'd like to have a way to let users pin down a version of the C++ toolchain
that we know works and use that.  Is there a way to do that in R?

I wouldn't be averse to letting users try whatever the hell they
want to install easily, but I'd like to have a set of very specific
instructions that are guaranteed to work.  I don't care if they're long.
Automateable is better, as Andrew keeps saying.

- Bob

remove.packages("rstan")
Sys.setenv(R_MAKEVARS_USER = "foobar")
Sys.setenv(R_MAKEVARS_SITE = "foobar")
options(repos = c(getOption("repos"), rstan = "http://wiki.rstan-repo.googlecode.com/git/"))

> 2b.  Fix a particular Rcpp version.
>
> Is there a way to use a version of Rcpp other than the most recent
> without interfering with the rest of the user's environment?  If so,
> I'd like to freeze Rcpp versions until we know more recent ones work.

You can fairly easily require a minimum version of Rcpp or any package. But I don't think you can require a maximum version or a particular version on CRAN. There is

http://rstudio.github.io/packrat/

but that is more for joint development. I don't think it is good form or practice to try to dictate what Rcpp people use. There are like 160 R packages that use Rcpp in some way and it is quite possible that one of them needs functionality in whatever the latest version of Rcpp is. But as long as we are spending money on bodyguards for conferences anyway ...

> 2c.  Fix a particular C++ toolchain.
>
> I'd like to have a way to let users pin down a version of the C++ toolchain
> that we know works and use that.  Is there a way to do that in R?

I don't know of any toolchain that is incapable of working except for the Compiler Suite Formerly Known as Sun Studio, which in fairness didn't work even before it got Oracled.

CRAN itself has started checking packages with clang on !Windows

http://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_flavors.html#r-devel-linux-x86_64-debian-clang

But you can't say, "just use clang++" because it is hard to install on Windows. Nor can you say "just use g++" because there really is no such entity. What is symlinked as g++ on Xcode is really llvm-g++-4.2 and what is called g++ on Windows is really mingw and based on g++-4.6. Neither are really supported by what would be considered upstream g++.

So, at a minimum, you are left with saying "just use X on platform Y". But I still think that is a bad idea. You need people to try the software with as many compilers as possible in order to find bugs.

> I wouldn't be averse to letting users try whatever the hell they
> want to install easily, but I'd like to have a set of very specific
> instructions that are guaranteed to work.  I don't care if they're long.
> Automateable is better, as Andrew keeps saying.

I think we only have a few systematic problems on stan-users
Stuff like -g on Windows which prevents stanc and some models from compiling
OS / Xcode versions
I almost never have compiler problems. Not that I am representative but it implies that the problems are less with Stan than with the users' environments. And they wouldn't be major problems if we had binary installs.

Ben
