Using p as probability of success and r as number of failures until the
experiment is stopped as wikipedia does, we have:

(1) The parametrization in this patch uses
neg_binomial (eta, phi)
with link-function exp(eta)=mu

where p=mu/(mu+phi)
r = phi
and
MEAN = mu
VARIANCE = mu +mu^2/phi

(2) Gelman's book is
neg_binomial (a, b)
where r=a
p=b/(b+1)
and
MEAN = ab
VARIANCE = ab(b+1)

(3) The other parametrization I suggest in the future is:
neg_binomial (mu, phi)
where p=mu/(mu+phi)
r = phi
and
MEAN = mu
VARIANCE = mu +mu^2/phi

(note (3) is for (1) as poisson_log is for poisson_log_log)

(1) is used for GLM, is the parametrization used by Nelder, J.A. &
Wedderburn, R.W.M. (1972). Generalized linear models.
Also used in bayesian inference:
http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bayesm/bayesm.pdf (page 71)

(3) seems to be useful when we have a negative binomial response
variable. See
http://doingbayesiandataanalysis.blogspot.com.br/2012/04/negative-binomial-reparameterization.html
It might not be the best practice (if there's best here anyway). I'm not
sure about this because I almost only work with regression this days,
so, this is grey area for me.

(2) I don't know about this one, maybe some people prefer it for uses
like in case (3), or maybe is used as some prior. I haven't read the
whole Bayesian Data Analysis yet and I didn't seem an example there
about it.

This paper uses yet another parametrization in section 4
http://www.johndcook.com/negative_binomial.pdf

About the nomenclature of phi (or r) parameter, I really don't know,
people call it, inverse dispersion, others overdispersion and so on. I
prefer inverse dispersion or something like that 'cause as you see
parametrization (1) and (3), as phi increases, variance decreases. But
in wikipedia parametrization, as r increases, variance increases (this
is because mine set the mean fixed, while Wikipedia's set p fixed) so
maybe that's why overdispersion is somewhat more popular.

Or we could just call it shape since it's same name used for alpha in
the manual (since alpha=r=phi).

About the name of the distribution, whatever is more in the current
standard of Stan, is better for me.

>     I'd like to freeze Rcpp versions until we know more recent ones work.
>
>
> You can fairly easily require a minimum version of Rcpp or any package. But I don't think you can require a maximum
> version or a particular version on CRAN. There is
>
> http://rstudio.github.io/packrat/
>
> but that is more for joint development. I don't think it is good form or practice to try to dictate what Rcpp people
> use. There are like 160 R packages that use Rcpp in some way and it is quite possible that one of them needs
> functionality in whatever the latest version of Rcpp is. But as long as we are spending money on bodyguards for
> conferences anyway ...
>
>     2c.  Fix a particular C++ toolchain.
>
>     I'd like to have a way to let users pin down a version of the C++ toolchain
>     that we know works and use that.  Is there a way to do that in R?
>
>
> I don't know of any toolchain that is incapable of working except for the Compiler Suite Formerly Known as Sun Studio,
> which in fairness didn't work even before it got Oracled.
>
> CRAN itself has started checking packages with clang on !Windows

> there really is no such entity. What is symlinked as g++ on Xcode is really llvm-g++-4.2 and what is called g++ on
> Windows is really mingw and based on g++-4.6. Neither are really supported by what would be considered upstream g++.
>
> So, at a minimum, you are left with saying "just use X on platform Y". But I still think that is a bad idea. You need
> people to try the software with as many compilers as possible in order to find bugs.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: encapsulating install in RStan?
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, February 16, 2014 11:30:00 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> (Ben --- would you mind helping Andrew fix his install.  I'm
> lost in all the suggestions that have gone by.)

I'm not that helpful with Macs, but it would seem that he just needs to agree to the license before trying to do anything involving compilation.

> Whether they should or not, I think people would install
> our binaries.  I installed WinBUGS and JAGS binaries outside
> of CRAN.  At the very least we could get Andrew out of the
> hole he's in.   It's not like we couldn't put nasty stuff in
> our source, so they shouldn't trust building it themselves
> any more.

You can do

R CMD INSTALL --build rstan*

on any platform to build a binary for that platform. We just need some place to put them.

> Now, onto specifics.
>
> 2a.  Do we somehow then need to add the makevars back in
> to deal with the Rcpp issue?

"The" Rcpp issue at the moment (not building with llvm-g++-4.2) is probably going to be short-lived. As far as I understand, that is a problem with compiling models, rather than installing the rstan package. But at the moment, I guess you have to (and want to) specify CXX = clang++ in Makevars before trying to compile a model.

> 2b.  I was hoping we could fix an Rcpp for Stan, not for
> all of R.  I hate hate hate all the dependencies introduced
> by the way R (and Linux apparently) manage installs.   We've had no
> end of trouble with modified versions of things outside of our
> control breaking our builds.

The only thing that I know of that does this is packrat, which I mentioned earlier

http://rstudio.github.io/packrat/

The package management of Debian, which CRAN is based on, is widely considered to be first-rate. I have about 1900 libraries on my laptop. I update them every day or two if new versions are available. It mostly works fine and it gets fixed in a day or two when it is broken.

> There may be 160 packages that use Rcpp, but my guess is that
> they're breaking all the time because their tests aren't thorough
> enough.  Just a guess.  Either that, or we're doing something really
> wrong in our use of Rcpp compared to the 160 other packages that
> got it right.

They aren't breaking that often because CRAN won't permit a new Rcpp that breaks packages that depends on it. We just aren't covered by that policy because we aren't on CRAN. They thought they had it before the latest release

http://lists.r-forge.r-project.org/pipermail/rcpp-devel/2014-January/007048.html

although the thing with lists and llvm-g++-4.2 slipped through because it wasn't a compiler / OS that they had access to.

> 2c.  This answers my earlier question about just setting clang++
> on Windows.  Grr.  Arg.

Clang++ on Windows is much farther behind than it is on Mac / Linux. It might not be any better than mingw at this point and at a minimum, it depends on the mingw headers currently. However, Stan with the mingw based on g++-4.8 is currently untenable. It takes more than 7.5 GB of memory to do some of the individual tests under src/test/unit/mcmc/hmc on a 64bit OS. We are surviving due to Rtools continuing to bundle a forked prerelease of mingw based on g++-4.6. If they ever bump, then Stan isn't going to be usable on Windows for a lot of people. Maybe by that time, one of the various refactorings will have fixed things or maybe clang++ will be ready.

Ben

Parameterization in BDA comes from negative binomial being a mixture of Poisson distributions with rates that follow Gamma(a,b). Thus the parameterization is similar to Student's t, where nu is the degrees of freedom of the Chi^2 scale mixing distribution.

I think it would be nice to use parameterizations in BDA. Maybe they are not always the best parameterizations for each modeling case, but as there is a strong connection between Stan and BDA, it would be nice if they were consistent on parameterizations.

Mine, too :-)  And I have BDA 3 in front of me right now.

>> (2) I don't know about this one, maybe some people prefer it for uses
>> like in case (3), or maybe is used as some prior. I haven't read the
>> whole Bayesian Data Analysis yet and I didn't seem an example there
>> about it.
>
> Parameterization in BDA comes from negative binomial being a mixture of Poisson distributions with rates that follow Gamma(a,b). Thus the parameterization is similar to Student's t, where nu is the degrees of freedom of the Chi^2 scale mixing distribution.
>
> I think it would be nice to use parameterizations in BDA. Maybe they are not always the best parameterizations for each modeling case, but as there is a strong connection between Stan and BDA, it would be nice if they were consistent on parameterizations.

All of our named distributions (with modifiers) are straight from BDA
other than normal, which uses scale rather than variance because Andrew
said he liked putting priors directly on scale.

For negative binomial, we use

   y ~ neg_binomial(alpha,beta)

with parameters:

    shape alpha > 0

    inverse scale beta > 0,

The mean and variance are:

   E[y] : alpha / beta

   var[y] : (alpha / beta^2) * (beta + 1)

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Current proposal for the function syntax and semantics
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Current proposal for the function syntax and semantics
messages.body_plain:
Looks great.  Having a language guy on the team certainly puts
Stan far ahead of the competition.  Some comments:

- I disagree with Marcus — having (transformed) data in scope may lead
to confusion down the road.  It’s easy enough to pass any necessary
objects into the function explicitly and it makes the users intent much clearer.

- Explicit container sizes, please!  They will make functions and models
that use them infinitely easier to understand and debug.

- I’m not sure I understand the bit about not allowing constrained inputs/outputs.
Does this mean, for example, that functions can’t take covariance matrices
as arguments? That seems like it would be pretty limiting.

- Given the special scope of “subroutines” can we give them a more
informative name?  Anything that makes it clear that they are the only
functions that have access to lp.  Maybe “submodel” or “model component”
or the like.  As Marcus noted, it may be best to avoid the use of “void”
if only to limit confusion.

>
> - I’m not sure I understand the bit about not allowing constrained inputs/outputs.
> Does this mean, for example, that functions can’t take covariance matrices
> as arguments? That seems like it would be pretty limiting.

No, it just means it can't specify them as arguments.

Note that none of the Stan functions that operate on
triangular or correlation matrices or positive-constrained
variables actually require arguments of that type.

The motivation is that only variables have those primitive
types and if you have any kind of expression, it's just too hard
to do the type inference.

So it's up to the function to deal with enforcing constraints.

>
> - Given the special scope of “subroutines” can we give them a more
> informative name?  Anything that makes it clear that they are the only
> functions that have access to lp.  Maybe “submodel” or “model component”
> or the like.

I was going to mention it but couldn't come up with a better name but I like "submodel", makes it clear not only what can be done but also what it's meant for.

"submodel" sounds good.

The basic idea in my mind is that "subroutines" applied to arguments
create statements, whereas functions applied to arguments create
expressions.

It only makes sense to me to call the subroutines in transformed parameters
or model blocks.  Or maybe even just in the model block.

The other question is whether to allow functions to be used as statements,
and we'd want to do it in general.  It's allowed in languages like C/C++/Java.
The only use case we have on the table is if the function threw an exception,
because there are no other side effects (other than log prob increments).

Thanks, Bob!

Function Block
* Looks great.
* Can we consider including other files? I'm envisioning a set of functions that someone might want to reuse / distribute. It'll essentially be allowing users to extend the language as a user base without hacking into Stan itself.

Syntax of Function Declarations and Definitions
* Looks great.
* I'm thinking that down the line we'd want to provide some way to debug functions. I know there are print statements and exceptions, but one of these days, we should really give a way for people to call their functions stand-alone and in a testing framework. I don't think this affects the design of the functions, but maybe the generated code?

Container Sizing in Argument and Return Types
* +1 for declared sizes (first option)

Variable Scope and Local Variables
* Looks good.

Return Statements
* Thanks for working it out. This is trickier than I imagined.
* Last bullet: what if we threw a fatal exception instead? Perhaps something like "User function is not specified properly. foo(x,y,z) with x=...,y=...,z=... does not return a value."

Input and Output Validation
* My guess is that not allowing constrained inputs / outputs is easier. Is that true?
* If that's true, my suggestion is to start by implementing that first. Allowing constrained variables looks like an extension to the language and would be backwards compatiable. We could get it out with no constrained variable declarations, and if that ends up hindering us(ers), we could work on constrained inputs / outputs.

Function application is an expression
* Looks good.

Subroutines
* Are these going to be declared in the same block as functions? From Marcus's and Michael's comments, it sounds like it should before the model block. Seems like a weird place to insert some code, though...
* I think if we had these in a separate block, we could get around the necessity of having to specify the return type of "void," but maybe I'm not seeing things clearly.
* Would it make sense to have a named subroutine (or "submodel") declared inside the model block? I'm looking at your example and think it really does belong within the model block, but I might be looking at this really shortsided.

Call by Constant Reference
* Looks good.

The easiest route would be to write a pre-processor
that read the files and concatenated them all together
to be passed into the parser.

The question is how we specify paths.  Right now, we have
the inconvenience that everything has to be run from
the home directory of Stan, so I suppose a relative path to
that would make sense?  Or we might do something clever with
stripping apart command line arguments to make it relative
to the file being processed?

> Syntax of Function Declarations and Definitions
> * Looks great.
> * I'm thinking that down the line we'd want to provide some way to debug functions. I know there are print statements and exceptions, but one of these days, we should really give a way for people to call their functions stand-alone and in a testing framework. I don't think this affects the design of the functions, but maybe the generated code?

I'm not sure most of our users will want to interact with
the C++ side alone.

Any idea how we'd do something like standalone testing of functions?
Ideally we'd have a nice unit testing framework, but that would require
a way to call the functions.  I could imagine writing something in the
simple Stan language that compiles to C++ and including some test
functions.  So users would have something like a test block after functions
that could optionally be called.

If we want to make data in scope, then the functions won't be
standalone, but will have to be coded as member functions on
a model.  It's one argument for

>
> Container Sizing in Argument and Return Types
> * +1 for declared sizes (first option)
>

I'm really surprised everyone wants that option.  Certainly
easiest to implement.  But it's not like the way either Eigen
or C++ writes functions to deal with containers, which contain
their own sizing information.  (And our variables all have their
own sizing built in because they're either std::vector or Eigen::Matrix.)

> Variable Scope and Local Variables
> * Looks good.
>
> Return Statements
> * Thanks for working it out. This is trickier than I imagined.
> * Last bullet: what if we threw a fatal exception instead? Perhaps something like "User function is not specified properly. foo(x,y,z) with x=...,y=...,z=... does not return a value."

We could do that by appending a final return statement and deal with
the "function not reachable" warning messages we'll get under compile for when they
do specify returns.  Or we could do the full analysis of functions to only add
it if there's not a final return somewhere (that is, look at the end of each
statement and add an exception throw if there's not a return).  I'd think rather
than doing that, we might just want to do a test at compile time and have them
rewrite the function.

> Input and Output Validation
> * My guess is that not allowing constrained inputs / outputs is easier. Is that true?

It's not only easier, it goes along with how we've done functions
already.  You'll note that things like bernoulli_log don't take
constrained inputs.

It's partly because at runtime, the C++ translation of a Stan type
is unconstrained.  That is, a real<lower=0,upper=1> just translates
to a double type.

We could have constrained inputs or outputs in the function specs and
then automatically enforce those constraints.  But you'd still be able
to pass in any old expression, not just a variable declared as that type.
That is, if I had a function declared

  real foo(real<lower=0,upper=1> theta);

then I could do something like this:

  real x;
  real y;
  ...
  y <- foo(x);

and then foo() would check that x is between 0 and 1.

> * If that's true, my suggestion is to start by implementing that first. Allowing constrained variables looks like an extension to the language and would be backwards compatiable. We could get it out with no constrained variable declarations, and if that ends up hindering us(ers), we could work on constrained inputs / outputs.
>

It's not that big a deal one way or the other.  The code
to do all the constraint checks is there already.

> Function application is an expression
> * Looks good.
>
> Subroutines
> * Are these going to be declared in the same block as functions? From Marcus's and Michael's comments, it sounds like it should before the model block. Seems like a weird place to insert some code, though...

I was planning on having everything up top and not depending on
data.  So yes, that was my proposal.

One problem with allowing dependence on data variables (not hard
to implement with members) is that we'd probably want to allow functions
to be called in transformed data and allow them to be defined in terms
of transformed data.  So you'd want to allow functions to be declared before
trnasformed data AND after transformed data.

I have a pretty strong preference to just put them all at the top and not
let them depend on data.  That would also make standalone debugging a lot
easier.

> * I think if we had these in a separate block, we could get around the necessity of having to specify the return type of "void," but maybe I'm not seeing things clearly.

Let's just forget I ever mentioned "void".  It's not necessary
no matter where they go.  It was just there in my mind for symmetry
with the C++ that gets generated.  But I can generate it in C++ w/o
having it be there in Stan.

> * Would it make sense to have a named subroutine (or "submodel") declared inside the model block? I'm looking at your example and think it really does belong within the model block, but I might be looking at this really shortsided.

I think of the functions as more outside the whole
model --- as you say, we may want to include them.

No reason to put them in the model block.  The model
block will use them, but I don't see any reason to declare
or define the functions or submodels there.

- Bob

messages.subject: [RFC] Convergence test
messages.body_plain:
Here is a proposal I have been playing with for testing convergence. Let me know what you think.

As I understand it, the objections in BDA to testing a null hypothesis of convergence are
This null hypothesis is presumably false so there is no point in testing it
(corollary of 1) Even if such a test is statistically significant, the difference between the simulated distribution of the quantity of interest and the theoretical distribution of the quantity of interest may be substantively negligible so what you really need is a loss function rather than a hypothesis test
Almost all of the tests in the coda and boa R packages operate on the margins but are not independent, so you aren't testing a null hypothesis of convergence anyway
I think each of these objections (plus a few more) can be overcome, at least for Stan. This paper by Rizzo and Székely (2010)

https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdfview_1/euclid.aoas/1280842151

generalizes the (M)ANOVA test with an index parameter alpha on the (0,2] interval. Iff alpha = 2, then the test simplifies to a (M)ANOVA test of equality of means across groups (or chains in the MCMC context). If alpha is on the (0,2) interval, then the test is consistent for a more general test that the groups (chains) have the same distribution (not required to be multivariate normal). It produces average between-group (B) and within-group distances (W) that are similar to the average between-group and within-group sum of squares in an ANOVA decomposition (or Rhat), although the resulting "F-statistic" is not exactly distributed F under the null hypothesis of no group-wise differences in distributions, so you have to do permutations to get p-values. In any event, this test is implemented in the disco() function in the energy R package.

However, this test presumes the realizations in each group are independent, which is not true for realizations from the same Markov chain. One could just ignore this problem and construct something similar to to the multivariate Brooks-Gelman-Rubin statistic with sqrt(T / W) where  T = (n - 1) / n * W + 1 / n * B to obtain a conservative loss function but that suffers from the same problem as the actual multivariate Brooks-Gelman-Rubin statistic in that it is hard to interpret as a scale factor of anything in particular.

Alternatively, one could thin the chains so that approximate independence of retained draws is a reasonable assumption and obtain the p-value for a test of the null hypothesis that all the chains have the same distribution. To do this, we can use the distance correlation concept of Székely, Rizzo, and Bakirov (2007)

https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdfview_1/euclid.aos/1201012979

which has the property that two possibly multivariate random variables A and B are independent iff the distance correlation between them is zero. We can estimate the distance correlation at time t by rowwise stacking the m draws at time t into the matrix A and rowwise stacking the m draws at time t - j into the matrix B for some j > 0 lags (the columns of both A and B are the posterior parameters). There is a bias-corrected version of the distance correlation estimator in the bcdcor() function in the energy package for R. We can then plot nonparametric curves of these distance correlations over time by j to see what lag length renders the draws essentially independent. This particular graph is fairly easy to interpret, such as in the case of the leuk model from the BUGS examples:

 <https://lh5.googleusercontent.com/-BKj57V8UKoI/Uwu-f2oCI9I/AAAAAAAAANk/l7SUQHqiXGw/s1600/leuk.png>
This plot is pretty typical of those in the BUGS corpus when the MCMC goes well in that it
exhibits declining dependence during the warmup period
exhibits fairly constant dependence after the warmup period
exhibits essential independence after a handful of lags (and this might improve once we bump the target acceptance rate up)
In this case, it looks like we need to thin by retaining every third or fourth draw. If so, the resulting convergence test is

> convergence(leuk, thin = 4, R = 100)
[1] "Multivariate loss = 1"
disco(x = mat, factors = chain_id, distance = FALSE, R = R)

Distance Components: index  1.00
Source                 Df   Sum Dist  Mean Dist    F-ratio    p-value
factors                20   36.90887    1.84544      0.956    0.54455
Within               5229 10095.38503    1.93065
Total                5249 10132.29390

With Stan, I can get about 75% of the BUGS models to fail to reject a null hypothesis of convergence. This test does not seem to depend heavily on the number of parameters (and other monitored quantities) --- except in the time and RAM needed to conduct it --- because while the absolute Euclidean distance between draws tends to increase as the dimensionality increases, the ratio of average between-chain distance to the average within-chain distance should be about 1.0 regardless of the dimensionality. The leuk model has 53 parameters.

I think this procedure is favorable when considering the limitations of the marginal Rhat and n_eff, which
presumes adequate mixing
looks only at mean differences
assumes the posterior distribution is approximately normal
yields a different n_eff for each margin
makes it hard to make a conclusion about convergence when a few Rhats are not <= 1.1
The last point is emphasized in a largely unknown AFAIK Political Analysis paper by Jeff Gill

http://www.artsci.wustl.edu/~jgill/papers/converge_gill.pdf

that shows due to the parameter dependence that evidence of nonconvergence on any margin is evidence of nonconvergence jointly in MH and Gibbs samplers. Thus, you really want to make a decision about whether to declare convergence based on some other criterion --- like the one I am outlining which I think overcomes Gill's criticisms too --- and then use the marginal Rhat for the quantity of interest of the model.

FWIW, the dependence plot for the similar leukfr model illustrates some problem:

 <https://lh6.googleusercontent.com/-VBx6ZjjiERI/UwvHiTzpHCI/AAAAAAAAAN0/_GB0h6ei7lc/s1600/leukfr.png>
Here, it looks as if something went wrong in the warmup phase, which resulted in an increase in the dependence as soon as we started retaining the draws. And the dependence is fading slowly so that the chains would have to be heavily thinned to test the null hypothesis of convergence. You still need to have rstan installed (from source) in order to use those binary models, so that wouldn't solve our installation problems. It would help in the sense that it obviates the need for every user to (inefficiently) write their own regression model. But we would have to make each binary model for both Windows and Mac (and possibly every variant thereof). The approach I was taking with the rstanarm package was to create the binary models once when the package was installed, which accomplishes about the same thing. In principle, we could split the rstan package into two one which had stanc and the stuff you need to compile a .stan model and one with the class definitions and stan(), sampling(), optimizing(), traceplot(), etc. Then, people could execute models someone else wrote even if they couldn't or wouldn't compile anything. But the most universal approach would be to use the intermediate representation of LLVM to distribute models that can be run in Chrome or any browser if they were converted to javascript via emscripten. That would allow people to do models without compiling or even being able to do R or Python. The compilation part mostly works now but we need a browser-based interface to call a CmdStan model.

Ben

messages.subject: Sobol sequences
messages.body_plain:
One issue that we have is that for a relatively small number of chains, randomly generating initial values on the (-a,a) interval in the unconstrained space doesn't necessarily create very overdispersed chains. One way to mitigate this would be to use a Sobol sequence

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobol_sequence

of initial values on the (-a,a)^K cube. This is relatively easy to do in the RStan context via a function like this

stopifnot(require(rstan))
stopifnot(require(randtoolbox))

sobol_init <- function(object, chains, lower = -2, upper = -lower, ...) {
  stopifnot(is(object, "stanfit"))
  n <- get_num_upars(object)
  x <- qunif(sobol(n, dim = chains, init = TRUE, ...),
             min = lower, max = upper)
  param_dims <- object@.MISC$stan_fit_instance$param_dims()
  pars <- names(param_dims)
  skeleton <- rstan:::create_skeleton(pars, param_dims)
  return(apply(x, MARGIN = 2, FUN = function(y) {
    r <- relist(y, skeleton)
    r <- r[sapply(r, FUN = function(z) all(!is.na(z)))]
    constrain_pars(object, unlist(r))
  }))
}

which returns a list of length chains with overdispersed starting values in the constrained parameter space.

But it would be better if we could "upstream" this to Stan. There is BSD-licensed C++ code for Sobol sequences at

http://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~fkuo/sobol/

but it would take some doing to rewrite the administrative stuff to not write to a file but instead keep the parameters x chains matrix in memory so that it can be used for starting values.

Sobol sequences would also be necessary if we ever want to do quasi Monte Carlo integration, which I have been talking about with Andrew for marginal maximum likelihood.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Feb 24, 2014, at 10:54 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Here is a proposal I have been playing with for testing convergence. Let me know what you think.

I think you need feedback from people who know more stats than me!

You should write all these contributions up as papers.  I think a wider
audience than the stan-dev list would be interested.

> With Stan, I can get about 75% of the BUGS models to fail to reject a null hypothesis of convergence.

If I'm counting negations properly, that means 25% of the BUGS models
do reject the null hypothesis of convergence?  That's bad, right?

>  This test does not seem to depend heavily on the number of parameters (and other monitored quantities) --- except in the time and RAM needed to conduct it --- because while the absolute Euclidean distance between draws tends to increase as the dimensionality increases, the ratio of average between-chain distance to the average within-chain distance should be about 1.0 regardless of the dimensionality. The leuk model has 53 parameters.
>
> I think this procedure is favorable when considering the limitations of the marginal Rhat and n_eff, which
> 	• presumes adequate mixing
> 	• looks only at mean differences
> 	• assumes the posterior distribution is approximately normal
> 	• yields a different n_eff for each margin
> 	• makes it hard to make a conclusion about convergence when a few Rhats are not <= 1.1

I thought Andrew's advice was that all Rhats should be below 1.05?

> The last point is emphasized in a largely unknown AFAIK Political Analysis paper by Jeff Gill
>
> http://www.artsci.wustl.edu/~jgill/papers/converge_gill.pdf
>
> that shows due to the parameter dependence that evidence of nonconvergence on any margin is evidence of nonconvergence jointly in MH and Gibbs samplers. Thus, you really want to make a decision about whether to declare convergence based on some other criterion --- like the one I am outlining which I think overcomes Gill's criticisms too --- and then use the marginal Rhat for the quantity of interest of the model.
>

If you've already declared convergence, why bother with Rhat?

N_eff is another matter, of course.

> FWIW, the dependence plot for the similar leukfr model illustrates some problem:
>
>
>

> Here, it looks as if something went wrong in the warmup phase, which resulted in an increase in the dependence as soon as we started retaining the draws. And the dependence is fading slowly so that the chains would have to be heavily thinned to test the null hypothesis of convergence. Nevertheless, the print output does not look that bad from the typical user's perspective

This is worrisome.  Though I'd say tau looks rather problematic in
this model, whatever it is.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, February 25, 2014 2:07:14 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What does "overdispersed" mean in general?

I just meant it in the BDA sense that you want the chains to start at overdispersed points so that Rhat and other convergence-related things are conservative. A low-discrepancy sequence is consistent with that sense of overdispersed because the points are constructed so that the chains are "evenly" distributed throughout the (-a,a)^K cube.

> Is it that
> you want pairwise distances to be very large while remaining
> in the (-a,a)^K cube?  And still presumably having some
> degree of randomness?

You can add randomness to it if you want, although it isn't so necessary. In addition to the distance thing, the columns (chains) are essentially uncorrelated, even without randomness.

> Randomly generating each dimension on (-a,a) should
> lead to fairly large expected distances between initial points,
> but some of the dimensions may be close.

For a large K and a small number of chains, you don't have a great probability of "surrounding" a particular parameter with the starting values are just random.

In addition, if given a Sobol sequence on (0,1)^K, we could automatically search for an "a" such that the density, gradients, etc. are sane to start with on the (-a,a)^K cube.

Ben

> On Feb 25, 2014, at 6:47 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > One issue that we have is that for a relatively small number of chains, randomly generating initial values on the (-a,a) interval in the unconstrained space doesn't necessarily create very overdispersed chains. One way to mitigate this would be to use a Sobol sequence
> >
> > http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sobol_sequence
> >
> > of initial values on the (-a,a)^K cube. This is relatively easy to do in the RStan context via a function like this
> >
> > stopifnot(require(rstan))
> > stopifnot(require(randtoolbox))
> >
> > sobol_init <- function(object, chains, lower = -2, upper = -lower, ...) {
> >   stopifnot(is(object, "stanfit"))
> >   n <- get_num_upars(object)
> >   x <- qunif(sobol(n, dim = chains, init = TRUE, ...),
> >              min = lower, max = upper)
> >   param_dims <- object@.MISC$stan_fit_instance$param_dims()
> >   pars <- names(param_dims)
> >   skeleton <- rstan:::create_skeleton(pars, param_dims)
> >   return(apply(x, MARGIN = 2, FUN = function(y) {
> >     r <- relist(y, skeleton)
> >     r <- r[sapply(r, FUN = function(z) all(!is.na <http://is.na>(z)))]
> >     constrain_pars(object, unlist(r))
> >   }))
> > }
> >
> > which returns a list of length chains with overdispersed starting values in the constrained parameter space.
> >
> > But it would be better if we could "upstream" this to Stan. There is BSD-licensed C++ code for Sobol sequences at
> >
> > http://web.maths.unsw.edu.au/~fkuo/sobol/
> >
> > but it would take some doing to rewrite the administrative stuff to not write to a file but instead keep the parameters x chains matrix in memory so that it can be used for starting values.

> > Sobol sequences would also be necessary if we ever want to do quasi Monte Carlo integration, which I have been talking about with Andrew for marginal maximum likelihood.

Yes, but the exceptions include cases where the model doesn't parse (fire), or is messup and and thereby excluded from test-models for other reasons. In addition, there are some models that probably would converge with more sane priors than inv_gamma(0,0) and what not. There weren't so many cases where I tried hard to get a seemingly reasonable BUGS model to converge and it wasn't happening.

> >  This test does not seem to depend heavily on the number of parameters (and other monitored quantities) --- except in the time and RAM needed to conduct it --- because while the absolute Euclidean distance between draws tends to increase as the dimensionality increases, the ratio of average between-chain distance to the average within-chain distance should be about 1.0 regardless of the dimensionality. The leuk model has 53 parameters.
> >
> > I think this procedure is favorable when considering the limitations of the marginal Rhat and n_eff, which
> >         • presumes adequate mixing
> >         • looks only at mean differences
> >         • assumes the posterior distribution is approximately normal
> >         • yields a different n_eff for each margin
> >         • makes it hard to make a conclusion about convergence when a few Rhats are not <= 1.1
>
> I thought Andrew's advice was that all Rhats should be below 1.05?

Andrew is a random variable. BDA III p. 287 was my source for 1.1.

> > The last point is emphasized in a largely unknown AFAIK Political Analysis paper by Jeff Gill
> >
> > http://www.artsci.wustl.edu/~jgill/papers/converge_gill.pdf
> >
> > that shows due to the parameter dependence that evidence of nonconvergence on any margin is evidence of nonconvergence jointly in MH and Gibbs samplers. Thus, you really want to make a decision about whether to declare convergence based on some other criterion --- like the one I am outlining which I think overcomes Gill's criticisms too --- and then use the marginal Rhat for the quantity of interest of the model.

>
> If you've already declared convergence, why bother with Rhat?
>
> N_eff is another matter, of course.

Yeah.

> >
> >
> >
> > Here, it looks as if something went wrong in the warmup phase, which resulted in an increase in the dependence as soon as we started retaining the draws. And the dependence is fading slowly so that the chains would have to be heavily thinned to test the null hypothesis of convergence. Nevertheless, the print output does not look that bad from the typical user's perspective
>
> This is worrisome.  Though I'd say tau looks rather problematic in
> this model, whatever it is.

It's a precision with a gamma(.001, .001) prior. This is among the likely sources of bad looking graphs I mentioned above.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] [RFC] Convergence test
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, February 25, 2014 2:21:28 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > Here is a proposal I have been playing with for testing convergence. Let me know what you think.
>
> I think you need feedback from people who know more stats than me!
>
> You should write all these contributions up as papers.  I think a wider
> audience than the stan-dev list would be interested.

Let's see how it goes first. The stat stuff can be worked, or really it already has by Rizzo and Székely (albeit not in reference to MCMC). What I think has happened is this:

In the beginning, there was a lot of FUD perpetuated by maximum likelihoodists about convergence of Bayesian models; e.g. what if you think your chains have converged and you publish the results but really your chains haven't converged yet and if you ran them a little longer they would converge to something that caused you to reach the opposite conclusion about your quantity of interest? And then there was BUGS, where you can burnin for hundreds of thousands of iterations and still maybe not feel confident about declaring convergence. And then there were a littany of convergence diagnostics that individually weren't conclusive and collectively could be contradictory. But BDA doesn't talk about many of them, so there is a generation of people that have basically come to an equilibrium where you verify that all the Rhats are sufficiently small and then decide that the chains have converged. And then you have the problem that Jeff Gill talks about where convergence is a joint concept but is judged marginally and you can easily get into a situation in hierarchical models where a minority of Rhats are not so small and can you rely on (functions of) the other parameters to make inferences?

So, what I think is needed is something where we can say something automatable "Do this, then that, and decide on convergence" that is backed by good statistical theory (i.e. it's joint rather than marginal, it tests for differences in distributions rather than merely differences in means,  it doesn't require multivariate normality, it exposes poor mixing rather than assuming adequate mixing, etc.).

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, February 25, 2014 3:06:42 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> I wouldn’t be surprised if lots of the BUGS models don’t converge, but
> we have to be really careful with multivariate tests like this.  There is
> not a lot of literature on multivariate MC-CLTs (i.e. none at all) but best
> case if we extrapolate the linear results then you’d have to take into
> account the differing ESS for the covariance estimates into the ANOVA
> which is going to be a nightmare.

Granted that the original paper was focused on the usual situation where someone is trying to decide if there are between-group differences in data and they don't explicitly talk about MCMC where the groups are chains. But aside from the fact that the test assumes independent observations, which isn't the case for a Markov chain and you have to thin enough for there to be approximate independence, I don't see anything about the paper that would make it inapplicable to Markov chain output.

For alpha = 2 and one variable, the test is equivalent to the ANOVA test, which uses CLT stuff to get the null distribution. But the main point is to use alpha < 2, so that you are testing differences in distribution rather than merely differences in means. Since the test explicitly doesn't require finite second moments, I'm not sure where the CLT would enter the consideration. In section 3.3, they do show that the asymptotic distribution of the test is a weighted sum of squared Gaussians, but they don't do anything with that except show that the sum diverges under the alternate hypothesis. To simulate the p-values, they do permutation tests, basically scrambling the groups structure and counting the proportion of times you get a more extreme statistic. So I'm not sure what we would need to be converging in distribution to a Gaussian in order for it to be a viable test?

Maybe you were saying that the multivariate MC-CLT enters somehow when deciding how much to thin the output before doing the test? I guess I'm distorting the size of the test a little bit by looking at the output to decide how much to thin, but I doubt that would be a major thing.

Ben

Mattering or better for what exactly? By construction, a Sobel is going to fill a hypercube more evenly than random or pseudorandom draws would. Almost.  The biggest question is what is the asymptotic distribution of a multivariate
Monte Carlo estimator?  The marginal variances (and diagonal elements of the
covariance matrix) will be the usual, true marginal variance / ESS, but it’s less
clear what the off-diagonal elements will be.  Even if the off-diagonals scale
as true covariance / ESS, we have n(n -1) / 2 ESSs to contend with and there’s
no strong theoretical argument (as far as I know) that motivates why they should
be the same.  And if they’re not the same then there’s no consistent way to define
a joint ESS for tests like yours.

In particular, if you’re going to claim a joint convergence diagnostic then it should
presumably be one that is invariant to parameter transformations.

The distance correlation measure of dependence is invariant to scale and rotation. But for other kinds of transformation, I guess it is up to the user as to what functions to monitor for between-chain differences when doing the tests.

Correct me if I am still misunderstanding, but I think you are saying that the within-chain degrees of freedom that the test is using should be equal to unknown ESS. So, like in the original example I gave

> convergence(leuk, thin = 4, R = 100)

[1] "Multivariate loss = 1"

disco(x = mat, factors = chain_id, distance = FALSE, R = R)

Distance Components: index  1.00
Source                 Df   Sum Dist  Mean Dist    F-ratio    p-

value
factors                20   36.90887    1.84544      0.956    0.54455

Within               5229 10095.38503    1.93065
Total                5249 10132.29390

you are saying that 5229 (21 * 1000 / 4 - 21) is not the right denominator for 10095.38503 / 5229 = 1.93065, which in turn is not the right denominator for 1.84544 / 1.93065 = 0.956 ?

If so, then I think there are two things to consider. First, the 5229 is a constant when they do the permutations to get the p-value, so I am not sure it makes a difference as to whether 5229 is really the ESS. Second, if you thin to the point that you think the retained draws are approximately independent, then I would guess that the ESS is approximately equal to the number of retained draws.

Then there is the question of whether what you are saying adversely affects the distance correlation vs. iteration plot used to decide the thin interval. I just did a lowess curve through the invisible points that represent the distance correlation at time t for lag length j. So that is not super-formal, reuses the data multiple times, depends on the bandwidth, etc. But I wasn't too worried about it initially. If you don't thin enough, then the within-chain distances are too small and the F-ratio is too big and you are more likely to make a Type I error. In which case, you would run it longer, thin it more, and likely land on your feet eventually.

Ben
